objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain every airworthiness requirement the CFI ACS lists, and teach a student a repeatable way to decide whether an airplane is airworthy for a given flight, including what to do with inoperative equipment.
why: Your students will copy the way you check an airplane. If you skip the logbooks or wave off a dead light, they will too. Aircraft used for instruction are often not under the instructor's maintenance control, so you can miss inoperative systems or overdue inspections unless you look [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. On the checkride you must locate the papers, decide airworthiness in the examiner's scenario and handle inoperative equipment while you explain it.

warmup: Think first: a student pilot meets you at the school's airplane and says "I checked it, it's airworthy." What three open questions would you ask to find out whether that is a real decision or a guess? Which of them would the student most likely be unable to answer?

key_terms.def: The aircraft conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation (14 CFR 3.5(a), as quoted in AFH 2-1). [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]
Issued for normal, utility, acrobatic, commuter and transport category aircraft, manned free balloons and special classes of aircraft. [[60:66|14 CFR 21.175(a)]]
Issued for primary, restricted, provisional and limited category aircraft, light-sport aircraft, experimental purposes and special flight permits. [[60:66|14 CFR 21.175(b)]]
A special airworthiness certificate for an aircraft that may not meet airworthiness requirements but is capable of safe flight, for a listed purpose. [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)]]
A legally enforceable FAA rule for an aircraft, engine, propeller or appliance with an unsafe condition. [[60:125|14 CFR 39.3]]
A different way to meet an AD, usable only after the manager of the office named in the AD approves it. [[60:126|14 CFR 39.19]]
Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin. Not regulatory; the FAA recommends reading it and taking it into account. [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]
Simple or minor preservation work and replacement of small standard parts, limited to the list in Part 43 Appendix A(c). [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]
The signed record entry by an authorized person that lets an aircraft fly again after maintenance or an inspection. [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]

An FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List plus the Letter of Authorization that lets a specific aircraft fly with listed items inoperative. Together they are a supplemental type certificate. [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)(2)]]
Kinds of Operations Equipment List: shows the kinds of operation (VFR, IFR, day, night) and the equipment each needs. No standard format. [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]]
MEL symbols for a maintenance procedure or an operations procedure that must be done before flight with the item inoperative. [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.4]]

chunks.title: The question you are really teaching: is this airplane airworthy?

body.p: General airworthiness requirements and compliance start with one word. Airworthy means two things: the airplane conforms to its type design, and it is in condition for safe operation [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. No person may operate a civil aircraft unless it is airworthy [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(a)]]. The owner or operator is primarily responsible for keeping it that way, including AD compliance [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]], but the pilot in command decides whether it is in condition for safe flight and must end the flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical or structural conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]].

Students learn a pile of separate rules and then cannot put them together at the airplane. Give them one repeatable sequence instead. The four questions below are this lesson's own teaching structure (application), built from the sourced checks:

head: Ask
Where the student looks
Source
rows: 1. Are the right papers on board?
Airworthiness certificate at the entrance, registration, operating limitations, weight and balance
2. Is it inspected and does it conform?
Logbooks or an airworthiness summary: annual, 100-hour if needed, ELT, transponder, ADs, Form 337s, life-limited parts
3. Is every required item working for THIS flight?
91.205, the equipment list and KOEL, then the MEL or 91.213(d)
4. Is it in condition for safe operation today?
The visual preflight from the AFM/POH, after the records review

callout.text: Instructor first: determine the aircraft's official airworthiness status before scheduled flights and before the preflight. Know the operator's procedures for reporting and correcting discrepancies, review the current discrepancy report, and settle any airworthiness question with maintenance before the preflight inspection [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

How to teach it: the AIH says to consider involving the learner in that status check and to stress that it manages the risk of failed equipment; in all cases, include the learner in risk management during dual instruction [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Ask open questions such as "How do you know this airplane is legal for tonight?" rather than "Is the annual current?" Closed yes or no questions test only rote learning [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

check.q: Your student finds a fresh annual sign-off and declares the airplane airworthy. Which half of the definition is still open, and how is it answered?
check.a: The records speak to conformity; the airplane must still be in condition for safe operation [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. That is answered by the visual preflight, which starts once the logbooks check out [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

chunks.title: K1a: Required certificates, where they go and when they expire

body.p: Location and expiration dates of required aircraft certificates. Two certificates must be within the aircraft: an appropriate and current airworthiness certificate, and an effective U.S. registration certificate (or, inside the United States only, the second copy of the registration application) [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]]. The airworthiness certificate must be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance, legible to passengers or crew [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]], and it must carry the aircraft's registration number [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]].

head: Certificate
How long it lasts
rows: Standard airworthiness (and special for primary, restricted, limited)

No printed expiry: effective while the aircraft is U.S.-registered and maintenance, preventive maintenance and alterations follow Parts 43 and 91 [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]] [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(1)]]. It transfers with the aircraft [[60:66|14 CFR 21.179]].
Special flight permit
For the period of time specified in the permit [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(2)]]
Special, light-sport category
Effective while it meets the light-sport eligibility criteria, conforms to its original or properly altered configuration, and has no unsafe condition [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(3)]]
Experimental (research and development, showing compliance, crew training, market survey)
3 years from issue or renewal unless the FAA sets a shorter period [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(4)]]
Experimental (amateur-built, exhibition, air racing and others)
Unlimited unless the FAA sets a period for good cause [[60:68|14 CFR 21.181(a)(5)]]
Certificate of Aircraft Registration (AC Form 8050-3)

Carried in the aircraft at all times [[1:236|PHAK 9-6]]. Expires seven years after the last day of the month of issue; renew with AC Form 8050-1B during the six months before expiry [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40]]
Second copy of the registration application (AC Form 8050-1)

Temporary authority inside the U.S. until the certificate arrives or the FAA denies the application; not available once 12 months have passed since the first application after the ownership transfer [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)]]

bullets: Registration also ends early: foreign registration, the aircraft totally destroyed or scrapped, the holder losing U.S. citizenship, or 30 days after the holder's death [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(a)]].

The FAA must be told. A paper certificate generally goes back to the Registry within 21 days of the registration ending (within 60 days of a holder's death, by the estate); an expired paper certificate is destroyed [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(b)(2)]] [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(b)(3)]].

The other papers on the AFH list: operating limitations (AFM/POH, placards, markings), current weight and balance, compass correction card if required, the external data plate, and a radio station license for flights outside the U.S. or airplanes over 12,500 pounds [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

callout.text: How to teach S1: stand at the airplane and let the learner find each paper, then read it aloud. Compare the N-number and serial number on the airworthiness certificate with the registration and the data plate, and ask what the Terms and Conditions box means. Logbooks are normally not kept in the airplane [[24:39|AFH 2-2]], so show where the operator keeps them.

check.q: On S1 the examiner asks why your airplane's standard airworthiness certificate, dated 1978, is still valid. What do you say?
check.a: It has no expiry date. It stays effective while the airplane is U.S.-registered and is maintained and altered under Parts 43 and 91, unless surrendered, suspended or revoked [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]] [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(1)]].

chunks.title: K4: Standard and special airworthiness certificates and their limits

body.p: Standard certificates are for aircraft type certificated in the normal, utility, acrobatic, commuter or transport category, as manned free balloons, or as special classes. Special certificates are for primary, restricted, provisional or limited category aircraft, the light-sport category, experimental purposes, and special flight permits [[60:66|14 CFR 21.175]]. The PHAK adds a quick visual cue: standard certificates are white and special certificates are pink [[1:73|PHAK 3-2]].

head: Certificate
Associated operational limitations (the ones students meet)
rows: Standard

91.205 equipment must be installed and operable [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]]; follow the AFM, markings and placards [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]]; annual and, when it applies, 100-hour inspections [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]]
Restricted

Only for the special purpose it is certificated for, such as crop dusting or banner towing; no carrying persons or property for compensation or hire (the special purpose work itself does not count); only crew, trainees and people essential to the special purpose may be carried; not over densely populated areas, in congested airways or near busy passenger airports unless authorized [[60:507|14 CFR 91.313(a)]] [[60:508|14 CFR 91.313(c)-(e)]]
Limited

No carrying persons or property for compensation or hire in operations that need a Part 119 certificate, are listed in 119.1(e), need fractional ownership management specifications, or are under parts 129, 133 or 137 [[60:509|14 CFR 91.315]]
Provisional
Flown only by eligible persons for listed purposes, and each person carried must be told the aircraft is provisionally certificated [[60:510|14 CFR 91.317]] [[60:511|14 CFR 91.317(j)(2)]]
Experimental

Only for the purpose issued; not over densely populated areas or in congested airways unless authorized; tell each person carried it is experimental; VFR day only unless authorized; tell ATC when using air traffic services [[60:511|14 CFR 91.319]]
Light-sport
Compensation only for towing, flight training, checking and testing, or listed aerial work; a condition inspection every 12 calendar months; comply with all ADs [[60:518|14 CFR 91.327]]
Special flight permit
Only the permitted flight, within its operating limitations and time period [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(2)]]

body.p: Two traps for students. First, 91.205 applies to powered aircraft with standard certificates [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]]; a special-certificate aircraft follows its own operating limitations. Second, an aircraft first issued an experimental certificate may not be flown with inoperative items unless its operating limitations specifically allow it [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]].

callout.text: How to teach it: start from the known, the white standard certificate in the trainer, then move to the unknown, a pink certificate and the operating limitations attached to it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. If a learner is buying a non-standard aircraft, the PHAK suggests asking the local FSDO about its requirements and limits [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

check.q: A club member offers your student a sightseeing ride in his restricted-category banner-tow airplane. What do you tell the student?
check.a: Only crew, crew trainees and people essential to the special purpose may be carried, and only for that purpose [[60:507|14 CFR 91.313(a)(1)]] [[60:508|14 CFR 91.313(d)]]. A sightseeing passenger is none of those.

body.p: Required inspections and aircraft logbook documentation are two halves of one skill: knowing what is due, then proving it was done. Start with what is due.

head: Inspection
When it is due
Source
rows: Annual

Within the preceding 12 calendar months, approved for return to service by a person authorized under 43.7. A 100-hour counts as an annual only if done by someone authorized to do annuals and entered as an annual
100-hour

Carrying any person other than a crewmember for hire, or giving flight instruction for hire in an aircraft that person provides. An annual also satisfies it. Up to 10 hours over only while en route to a place where it can be done, and those hours count toward the next 100
Progressive

A written request to the responsible Flight Standards office; a complete inspection within each 12 calendar months. If it stops, the annual is due within 12 calendar months, and the 100-hour within 100 hours, after the last complete inspection
ELT
Inspected within 12 calendar months after the last one; battery replaced after more than 1 cumulative hour of use or when 50 percent of its useful life has expired
Transponder
Tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months before it may be used
Altimeter, static system and encoder
Within the preceding 24 calendar months, for IFR in controlled airspace
Airworthiness limitations
Mandatory replacement times and inspection intervals in the manufacturer's airworthiness limitations section

body.p: Aircraft that carry a special flight permit, a current experimental certificate, a light-sport certificate or a provisional certificate are outside the annual and 100-hour rules [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(c)(1)]]. The annual is done by an A&P mechanic with an Inspection Authorization, the manufacturer or a rated repair station; the 100-hour may also be done by an A&P [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

callout.text: The instructor's own trap: the 100-hour rule turns on who provides the aircraft. If you give paid instruction in an airplane you provide, it needs the 100-hour; if the learner provides the airplane, the rule's instruction clause does not reach you [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. Say this out loud to every learner who later becomes an owner or an instructor.
Calendar months end on the last day of the month: 12 calendar months run from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

check.q: The ELT was last inspected on July 9, 2026. Your student says the next inspection is due by July 9, 2027. Is that right?
check.a: Not quite. The ELT inspection is due within 12 calendar months after the last one [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]], and calendar months run to the last day of the month [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]], so it is good through July 31, 2027.

chunks.title: K1b: Logbook documentation, and the logbook review with your student

body.p: Each airplane has airframe and engine logbooks, and sometimes propeller and appliance logbooks. The pilot should review them, or a summary of the airworthy status, before flight [[24:39|AFH 2-2]]. The AFH list: annual, 100-hour if for hire, transponder, static system and encoder, 30-day VOR check for IFR, ELT inspection and battery, life-limited parts, AD status, Form 337s and inoperative equipment [[24:40|AFH 2-3]].

head: Entry
What it must show
Source
rows: Maintenance or preventive maintenance
Description of the work, date completed, who did it, and the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving it. That signature approves only the work performed
Inspection
Type and extent, date and total time in service, signature, certificate number and kind; then either the airworthy statement or a statement that a dated list of discrepancies was given to the owner
Major repair or alteration
The entry plus the FAA form (Form 337)
AD status
For each AD: method of compliance, AD number and revision date, and for recurring ADs the time and date of the next action

bullets: Work records are kept until the work is repeated or superseded, or 1 year; total time, life-limited parts, inspection status, AD status and major alteration forms go with the aircraft when it is sold [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)]].
No one may fly an aircraft after maintenance until a person authorized under 43.7 approves it for return to service and the entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

If the work may have changed the flight characteristics, no passengers until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private certificate flies an operational check and logs it in the aircraft records [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]], unless ground tests show conclusively that nothing changed [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(c)]].

callout.text: The entry students misread: an inspection entry that says a list of discrepancies and unairworthy items has been provided means the aircraft was NOT approved for return to service [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)(5)]]. Look for later entries that clear each item. The owner keeps that list until the defects are repaired and the aircraft is approved [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(3)]].

How to teach it (demonstration-performance): explain the goal and the standard; demonstrate a full review out loud, starting at the last annual and working forward by total time; have the learner do the next review as soon as possible while you supervise; then evaluate together [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Use the real records of the airplane you will fly.

check.q: Reviewing the logbook, your student sees an alternator replaced last week with an A&P's signature and "returned to service." He says that proves the whole airplane is airworthy. Correct him.
check.a: The signature approves only the work performed [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)(4)]]. Airworthiness still needs a current annual, the other required inspections, AD status and a preflight [[24:40|AFH 2-3]].

body.p: Airworthiness Directives and Special Airworthiness Information Bulletins look alike to students, but one is law and one is advice. Teach Part 39 as a short list of questions, because that is how the rule is written.

head: Student question
Answer
Source
rows: What is an AD?
A legally enforceable rule for an aircraft, engine, propeller or appliance
When is one issued?
An unsafe condition exists and is likely in other products of the same type design
What if it is not done?
Operating the product is a violation, each time you operate it
Is it in the CFR book?
Yes, but not printed in the annual edition; each AD is published in the Federal Register as an amendment to 39.13
What if the part was modified?
The AD still applies; if the change stops you doing the AD as written, request an AMOC
Can I do it another way?
Propose an AMOC; use it only after the manager of the office named in the AD approves it
Can I fly to the shop?
The FSDO may issue a special flight permit unless the AD says otherwise, and may refuse if the aircraft cannot be moved safely
AD and service bulletin disagree?
Follow the AD

body.p: ADs come in two urgencies: emergency ADs that require compliance before further flight, and less urgent ones with a compliance period. A recurring AD has no overfly allowance unless the AD itself provides one [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]. An MEL cannot list equipment an AD requires to be operable unless the AD allows it [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(b)(2)]].

Special Airworthiness Information Bulletins (SAIBs) are not regulatory, but the FAA recommends reading them and taking them into account for safety. The PHAK's examples are SAIB CE-10-21 on propeller overspeed in piston airplanes [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]] and SAIB NE-11-15, which says 100VLL avgas is acceptable [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]].

callout.text: How to teach it: open the airplane's AD status record with the learner, pick one recurring AD and have them work out when it is next due from the record (91.417 requires that figure). Then ask why an SAIB might change how they fly, as the propeller overspeed SAIB does. Linking a paper to a flight decision is the correlation level, the goal of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

check.q: Your student reads an SAIB on the engine and says, "It is not an AD, so it does not matter." What do you teach?
check.a: It is not regulatory, but the FAA recommends that it be read and considered for safety of flight [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]. Talk through what it changes about inspections or procedures, and with the owner whether to act on it.

chunks.title: K1d: Special flight permits, purpose and procedure

body.p: Purpose and procedure for obtaining a special flight permit. A special flight permit is a special airworthiness certificate [[60:66|14 CFR 21.175(b)(4)]] for an aircraft that may not currently meet airworthiness requirements but is capable of safe flight [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)]].

bullets: Purposes: flying to a base for repairs, alterations or maintenance, or to storage; delivering or exporting; production flight testing; evacuating from areas of impending danger; customer demonstration flights in new production aircraft [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)]].

Overweight ferry: operation above maximum takeoff weight for flight beyond normal range over water or land without adequate landing facilities or fuel; the excess is limited to extra fuel, fuel-carrying facilities and navigation equipment [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(b)]].
Continuing authorization: some certificate holders get it in their operations specifications for flights to a maintenance base [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(c)]] [[60:79|14 CFR 21.197(c)(1)]].

body.p: Procedure: the applicant submits a statement giving the purpose, the proposed itinerary, the crew required, every way the aircraft does not comply with airworthiness requirements, any restriction the applicant considers necessary, and anything else the FAA needs to set operating limitations [[60:79|14 CFR 21.199(a)]]. The FAA may make or require inspections or tests [[60:79|14 CFR 21.199(b)]]. The local FSDO gives help and forms; an FAA inspector may inspect the aircraft or have an A&P or repair station do it, and that inspection is recorded in the aircraft records [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]. An AD-related permit uses the same 21.199 procedure [[60:126|14 CFR 39.25]].

bullets: Inoperative equipment may be flown under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].
An airplane overdue for its annual may ferry to the inspection under a permit, but ADs that are due must be complied with before the flight [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].
The permit lasts only for the period it specifies [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(2)]].

callout.text: Do not confuse the permit with the ELT ferry rule. An airplane with an inoperative ELT may be ferried from a place where repairs cannot be made to a place where they can, but only required crewmembers may be aboard [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]].

How to teach it: role-play the owner who wants to "just fly it over" to the shop. The learner must say what is out of compliance and why a permit, not a shortcut, is the legal path. Role playing is how instructional communication is first learned [[25:100|AIH 4-7]].

check.q: A hurricane is forecast for your field in two days. A club airplane's annual ran out last week. Is there a legal way to move it?
check.a: Yes. Evacuating aircraft from areas of impending danger is a listed purpose for a special flight permit [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)(4)]]. Apply through the FSDO with the 21.199 statement [[60:79|14 CFR 21.199(a)]].

body.p: Preventive maintenance is simple or minor preservation work and the replacement of small standard parts without complex assembly, limited to the items listed in Part 43 Appendix A(c) [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]] [[60:142|Part 43 App. A(c)]].

head: Question
Rule
Source
rows: Who may do it?

The holder of a Part 61 pilot certificate (other than sport pilot), on an aircraft that pilot owns or operates, not used under Part 121, 129 or 135. Part 61 pilot certificates include student and recreational [[60:194|14 CFR 61.5(a)(1)]]. A sport pilot only on an owned or operated light-sport aircraft
Who may sign it off?

A person with at least a private pilot certificate may approve the aircraft for return to service after doing it under 43.3(g). For a light-sport category aircraft the pilot owns or operates, at least a sport pilot certificate is enough
What goes in the record?
Description of the work, date completed, and the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving it
How must it be done?
Using the methods in the current manufacturer's maintenance manual or Instructions for Continued Airworthiness (or other acceptable methods), leaving the part at least equal to its original condition

bullets: On the list: removing, installing and repairing tires; servicing shock struts with oil or air; replacing bulbs, reflectors and lenses of position and landing lights; spark plugs; filter elements; batteries [[60:142|App. A(c)(1), (3), (17), (20)]] [[60:143|App. A(c)(23), (24)]].
Tray-mounted panel navigation and communication units may be swapped, but not autopilots, transponders or DME, and an operational check is required before use [[60:143|App. A(c)(31)]].

Off the list: hydraulic hose connections, wheels when a weight and balance computation is involved, and cowlings that need the propeller removed or flight controls disconnected [[60:142|App. A(c)(18), (19)]] [[60:143|App. A(c)(21)]].
Deactivating an inoperative system is not preventive maintenance [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

Updating an installed avionics database from the flight deck, with no disassembly and no tools, is not maintenance at all, provided the pilot follows the manufacturer's instructions [[60:131|14 CFR 43.3(k)]].

callout.text: How to teach it: use telling-and-doing. You tell and do, the learner tells while you do, then the learner tells and does [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. With the owner's permission, demonstrate one real task such as a landing light lens, write the entry together, then have the learner find the Appendix A paragraph that allows it. Make "Which paragraph?" the habit question before any tool comes out.

check.q: A student pilot owns her standard-category airplane and replaces a worn main tire herself. Can she approve it for return to service?
check.a: She may do the work under 43.3(g), but approving return to service after preventive maintenance needs at least a private pilot certificate [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]] [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]]. Someone authorized under 43.7, such as a mechanic, must approve it.

chunks.title: K3: Equipment requirements for day and night VFR

body.p: For a powered aircraft with a standard airworthiness certificate, the 91.205 instruments and equipment must be installed and in operable condition for the kind of operation flown [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]].

head: Day VFR, 91.205(b)
Night VFR adds, 91.205(c)
rows: Airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic direction indicator [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]
Approved position lights [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(2)]]

Tachometer; oil pressure gauge; temperature gauge for a liquid-cooled engine; oil temperature gauge for an air-cooled engine; manifold pressure gauge for an altitude engine [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]
An approved anticollision light system [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(3)]]
Fuel gauge for each tank; gear position indicator if retractable [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]
One electric landing light, if operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]]

Anticollision lights on small airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996; flotation gear and a signaling device if for hire beyond power-off gliding distance from shore [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11)-(12)]]
An adequate source of electrical energy for all installed electrical and radio equipment [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(5)]]
Safety belts; shoulder harnesses by date of manufacture; an ELT if 91.207 requires one [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(13)-(15)]]
One spare set of fuses, or three of each kind, accessible in flight [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(6)]]

body.p: If any light of the anticollision system fails, the flight may continue to a place where repairs can be made [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(3)]]. And 91.205 is only the operating-rule minimum: the AFM/POH equipment list, made during certification, shows what the airplane needs to be airworthy [[24:25|AFH 1-4]].

callout.text: How to teach it: skip the memory aid at first. Sit in the airplane and have the learner touch each 91.205(b) item, then ask what changes after sunset. Then open the equipment list and find the "C" items, which are required for certification. Going from the familiar panel to the unfamiliar list is the known-to-unknown strategy [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

check.q: On a night cross-country, one strobe of the anticollision system fails at an intermediate stop where no repairs are possible. What does 91.205 allow?
check.a: Operation may continue to a stop where repairs or replacement can be made [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(3)]]. Weigh the risk of flying on with it before deciding.

chunks.title: K3a, K3c: Flying with inoperative equipment without an MEL, and the KOEL

body.p: Flying with inoperative equipment is legal in only three ways: an MEL with its LOA, the 91.213(d) provision, or a special flight permit [[58:20|AC 91-67A 3.2]]. The PHAK says most pilots and operators use 91.213(d) because it is simple [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]], and it needs no application, written request or approval [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.1]]. It covers non-turbine airplanes, among others, but not turbine-powered airplanes [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(1)]] [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]].

head: 91.213(d) step
What it means
Source
rows: (d)(2) Is it required?

It may NOT be deferred if it is VFR-day type certification equipment; marked required on the equipment list or on the KOEL for this kind of operation; required by 91.205 or another Part 91 rule for this operation; or required by an AD
(d)(3) Remove or deactivate

Removed with the cockpit control placarded and the maintenance recorded under 43.9, or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative"; deactivation that involves maintenance is done and recorded under Part 43
(d)(4) Is it a hazard?
A certificated, appropriately rated pilot, or a person rated to maintain the aircraft, determines it is not a hazard
Result
The aircraft is considered to be in a properly altered condition acceptable to the Administrator

body.p: Kinds of Operation Equipment List (KOEL). Part 23 and 27 aircraft may have one. It names the kinds of operation the aircraft may fly (VFR, IFR, day, night) and the installed equipment that can affect an operating limitation. It has no standard format, so manufacturers present it in different ways. Equipment the KOEL requires for a kind of operation may not be deferred under 91.213 for that operation [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]]. The certification rule behind it: the equipment needed for each kind of operation requested (day VFR, night VFR, IFR) must be designed and installed for it [[60:116|14 CFR 23.2500(a)]].

Who does the work. The AC says repair, removal, deactivation or inspection must be done by a person authorized to do maintenance under 43.3 [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.2]]. Turning off a switch does not remove power. Deactivation is not preventive maintenance, and the person who approves the return to service makes the 43.9 entry; no one may fly without it [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].
Required discrepancy records or placards (no MEL):

bullets: Record: the decision sequence starts with an entry in the aircraft maintenance records [[58:26|AC 91-67A Figure 4-1]]; removal and deactivation are recorded under 43.9 [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.1]] [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

Placard: each inoperative item is marked, for example "inoperative", next to its control or indicator; any form, but legible, visible to the crew and not covering other controls [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]].

Follow-up: the owner has a deferred item repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]]; the inspector gives a signed, dated discrepancy list and placards each item allowed to stay inoperative [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]] [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.3]].

callout.text: Deferrals are for items found before flight. A failure in flight is handled with the AFM/POH procedures, not with a deferral [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

check.q: The POH's KOEL marks the pitot heat as required for IFR only. Your student plans a day VFR flight and finds it inoperative. Is the KOEL test passed, and are you done?
check.a: The KOEL does not require it for day VFR, so that test passes [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]]. You are not done: check the other (d)(2) tests, then the item must be deactivated and placarded, with any maintenance recorded, and a hazard determination made [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

chunks.title: K3b: Using an approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL)

body.p: Using an approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL) needs four things: an approved MEL for that aircraft; a Letter of Authorization from the responsible Flight Standards office in the aircraft; aircraft records available to the pilot that describe the inoperative items; and operation under every condition and limitation of the MEL and the LOA. The MEL and LOA together are a supplemental type certificate [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]]. An MEL may not include items essential under all conditions by the type certification rules, items an AD requires unless the AD allows it, or items Part 91 requires for specific operations [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(b)]].

bullets: Once an operator has an MEL and LOA, using the MEL becomes mandatory for that aircraft [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

The operator's MEL is based on the MMEL for the make, model and series; it may be more restrictive, never less [[58:10|AC 91-67A 1.8.13]]. Single-engine airplanes without their own MMEL may use the generic Single-Engine Airplanes MMEL [[58:14|AC 91-67A 2.1.2]].
The LOA goes to whoever has operational control. A dry lessee may not use the lessor's MEL [[58:21|AC 91-67A 3.3.3]].
The MEL and LOA must be accessible to the PIC, in print or digital form; a phone call or radio is not acceptable access [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1]].

MEL relief applies to items found up until takeoff, the moment power is applied for takeoff [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.1]]. A failure found during taxi may not be flown until the deferral, including any required inspection, is complete [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.2]]. A failure after takeoff is handled with the AFM/POH and recorded, then repaired or deferred before the next takeoff [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.3]].

head: Part of the MMEL page
Meaning
Source
rows: Column 1, repair category (A to D)
Not used for 91.213(a) MELs, but proviso repair intervals are. Repair by the proviso interval or the next required inspection, whichever comes first
Column 2, number installed
Quantity normally installed; a dash means variable
Column 3, number required for dispatch
Minimum that must work, if the remarks are met
Column 4, remarks or exceptions
Provisos, notes, "as required by 14 CFR" statements and (M) and (O) symbols
(M) and (O)
A maintenance or operations procedure that must be done before flight with the item inoperative
Triple asterisk (***)
An item not required by regulation, installed on some models

body.p: Required discrepancy records or placards (with an MEL): a means of recording discrepancies and corrective actions must be in the aircraft for the PIC; each inoperative item found gets an entry in the maintenance records, or in a discrepancy log kept as part of those records; and each inoperative item is placarded where practical next to its control or indicator [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.2]] [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.3]].

callout.text: An item not listed in the MEL as deferrable, such as a tachometer, flaps or a stall warning device, must be repaired before departure, or the aircraft flown on a special flight permit [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

check.q: Your student's club has an MEL and LOA for its Bonanza. A reading light fails on preflight. The student wants to use 91.213(d) because it is simpler. Can he?
check.a: No. With an MEL and LOA issued, use of the MEL is mandatory for that aircraft [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], and 91.213(d) applies only to operations not conducted under paragraph (a) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

chunks.title: R1: Inoperative equipment discovered before flight, the risk side

body.p: A legal deferral is not the same as a safe flight. When inoperative equipment is found before departure, the choices are to cancel, get maintenance first, or defer the item [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]], and deferral is not to be taken lightly, especially when other items are already inoperative [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Before flying with an inoperative item, the AC asks for a safety risk analysis of whether the aircraft and crew can do this operation in the expected conditions [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]:

bullets: Does the item, including how it failed, create a hazard? Is it needed for this operation?
How do several failed items interact?
Adverse weather and night operations.
Departure and destination airports, the en route environment, diversion and alternate options.
Extra workload from the inoperative item, crew fatigue and other human factors. [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]

body.p: Teach it with a real accident. In the AIH's Mooney case the pilot knew the vacuum pump had failed (an aircraft hazard) and that instrument conditions lay ahead (an environment hazard); the urge to get there added external pressure, and assuming he could fly with critical instruments inoperative added a pilot hazard. Catastrophic severity with occasional or probable likelihood put it in the high-risk box [[25:186|AIH 10-2]]. A minor fault also distracts: many accidents begin with something as small as a gauge reading wrong [[25:17|AIH 1-13]].

callout.text: How to teach it: change the scenario on purpose. The deferral that was fine for a 10 a.m. lesson is re-run when the student proposes a 5 p.m. return. Planned scenario changes are part of scenario-based training [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. Watch for external pressure: scheduling problems made worse by aircraft problems are a known learner stressor [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: The left position light is legally deferred for a day flight, but your student's return now lands 20 minutes after sunset. Which AC risk factor is this, and what is the fix?
check.a: Night operations [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]. Position lights are required at night [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(2)]], so the deferral no longer works: land before sunset or get the light repaired.

chunks.title: How to teach it, and what the examiner will see

body.p: The ACS Skills for this Task say you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to locate the papers (S1), decide airworthiness in the evaluator's scenario (S2) and apply inoperative-equipment procedures (S3). Build the lesson as a demonstration-performance block.

head: Phase
What you do with airworthiness
Source
rows: Explanation
State the objective (decide if this airplane is airworthy for this flight), the standard, and the safety points; invite questions
Demonstration
Do S1, S2 and S3 yourself out loud on the real airplane and records, in the same order you will expect from the learner; if you go off script, say so
Learner performance with supervision
The learner reviews the next airplane as soon as possible after your demonstration while you watch and comment
Evaluation
Collaborative critique: replay, reconstruct, reflect, redirect, then compare your assessment with theirs

bullets: S1: hand over the airplane, not a list. The learner finds and explains each certificate and paper, and says how long it lasts.
S2: give a non-flight scenario with a task narrative, desired outcome and planned changes, such as a records set with one buried problem [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].
S3: give an inoperative item and make the learner walk the 91.213(d) or MEL path to a decision, then change one fact (day to night, VFR to IFR) and run it again.
Grade the decision-making as well as the facts: explain, practice, then manage-decide without your help [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].
Ask questions that make the learner decide, not recite [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

callout.text: Risk of teaching it: if you clear an airplane for the learner, the learner learns that someone else decides airworthiness. The AIH says to include the learner in risk management in all cases, and to consider involving the learner in the airworthiness status check [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: Your learner can recite every inspection interval but cannot say whether the school airplane may fly tonight. Which learning level is that, and what is the goal?
check.a: Rote, the ability to repeat without being able to apply it [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]. The goal of aviation instruction is correlation [[25:66|AIH 3-15]], so give scenarios that force a decision.

body.p: These are the airworthiness mistakes the sources warn about. Watch for each one during records reviews and preflights.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Checking only 91.205
"It is not on the 91.205 list, so we can go"
Run all four (d)(2) tests, including the equipment list, the KOEL and ADs [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]
Self-deactivation
Pulls a breaker, sticks on tape marked INOP and goes
An authorized person deactivates and makes the 43.9 entry; deactivation is not preventive maintenance [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]
Deferring an in-flight failure
Something fails in cruise and the student plans to "defer it" and keep going
In flight, use the AFM/POH; record it after landing and repair or defer before the next takeoff [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]] [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.3]]
Reading the date, not the statement
Sees a recent annual and stops reading
Check for the discrepancy-list statement [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)(5)]]
Overflying a recurring AD
"The 100-hour gets 10 extra hours, so the AD does too"
No overfly allowance unless the AD itself grants one [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]
Work outside Appendix A
A pilot owner replaces a hydraulic hose or a wheel that needs a weight and balance computation
Both are excluded from the preventive maintenance list [[60:142|App. A(c)(18)]] [[60:143|App. A(c)(21)]]
MEL taken lightly
Finds a failure during taxi and departs, planning to write it up later
No takeoff until the deferral process is complete [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.2]]
No placard
The item is legally deferred but nothing marks it in the cockpit
Placard it next to the control or indicator [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]]

callout.text: Fix errors with questions, not lectures: "Which rule lets this item be inoperative? Who signed for it? What changes tonight?" Questions should focus the learner on the decision-making process [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

check.q: Your student finds the stall warning dead on preflight, pulls its breaker and writes INOP on masking tape. Name two errors.
check.a: Deactivation must be done by an authorized person with a 43.9 entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]; and a stall warning device is the PHAK's example of an item not deferrable under an MEL [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], so check the equipment list before any deferral.

scenario.title: Dana's new airplane
scenario.setup: Today is October 27, 2026. Dana, a private pilot, bought a 1979 Piper Warrior (standard category, non-turbine, no MEL) on September 2 and hires you for paid instruction in it. The registration application went in on September 5, and the second copy is in the airplane. The airframe log shows an annual signed November 14, 2025 with the airworthy statement. The transponder test is dated August 12, 2024. A recurring AD must be done every 100 hours; the AD record shows it last done at 2,113.5 tach hours and the tach now reads 2,216.0. Last week an A&P replaced the vacuum pump and signed the entry. Dana wants you to approve the airplane for a lesson today.

questions.q: Does Dana's airplane need a 100-hour inspection because you are paid to teach in it?
questions.a: No. The instruction clause applies to flight instruction for hire in an aircraft that the instructor provides [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. Dana provides it, and no one is carried for hire. It still needs its annual [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

questions.q: Is the registration in order for today's local flight?
questions.a: The second copy of the application is temporary authority inside the United States until the certificate arrives or the application is denied [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)(1)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]]. For a local flight it is in order.

questions.q: What does the August 12, 2024 transponder date mean today?
questions.a: The test is good for 24 calendar months, through August 31, 2026, so the transponder may not be used until it is tested again [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]] [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. Plan accordingly and have it tested.

questions.q: Dana says the AD is "only 2.5 hours over, and inspections get 10 hours of grace." How do you answer?
questions.a: Due at 2,113.5 + 100 = 2,213.5; 2,216.0 - 2,213.5 = 2.5 hours overdue. A recurring AD has no overfly allowance unless the AD grants one [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]], and every flight is a violation [[60:125|14 CFR 39.9]]. No lesson today; a special flight permit to the shop is possible unless the AD says otherwise [[60:126|14 CFR 39.23]].

questions.q: Dana points to the vacuum pump entry as proof the airplane is airworthy. What do you teach?
questions.a: The A&P's signature approves only the work performed [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)(4)]]. Airworthiness rests on the whole record: annual, required inspections, AD status, and then the preflight [[24:40|AFH 2-3]].

questions.q: How would you run this review as a lesson rather than a lecture?
questions.a: Explain the goal, demonstrate one section aloud, then let Dana do the rest while you supervise [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Close with a collaborative critique: Dana replays what he found, then you reconstruct and redirect toward an airworthiness summary sheet he keeps [[25:136|AIH 6-5]].

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to "locate and describe airplane airworthiness and registration information." This Task has no numeric tolerance; the examiner watches you find the airworthiness certificate at the entrance and the registration [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203]], explain how long each lasts [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(1)]] [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40]], and point out the other required papers [[24:41|AFH 2-4]], all while teaching.
skills.practice: Brief a friend who plays a new student at three different airplanes, including one with a special certificate. Time yourself and cite the rule for each paper.

skills.do: The ACS says you "determine the airplane is airworthy in the scenario given by the evaluator." Expect a records set or a story with a hidden problem. Work it in order: papers, inspections and AD status, required equipment for the flight, then condition, and state a clear yes or no with the rule [[24:40|AFH 2-3]] [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].
skills.practice: Have another applicant plant one problem in a real logbook set (an expired transponder test, a discrepancy-list annual, an overdue recurring AD) and find it out loud.

skills.do: The ACS says you "apply appropriate procedures for operating with inoperative equipment in a scenario given by the evaluator." Walk the 91.213(d) sequence or the MEL path out loud: required or not, the maintenance action, the placard and record, the hazard determination, and a risk analysis for this flight [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]] [[58:26|AC 91-67A Figure 4-1]] [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]].
skills.practice: Pick five items in your training airplane's equipment list and run each through Figure 4-1 for day VFR, then again for night VFR.

quiz.q: Besides being current and appropriate, what must a U.S. standard airworthiness certificate show to satisfy 91.203(a)(1)?
options: The date of the last annual inspection signed by an IA
The current owner's name and permanent mailing address
The registration number assigned to the aircraft
The aircraft's maximum gross weight
quiz.why: Each U.S. airworthiness certificate used to comply must have on it the registration number assigned under part 47 or 48 [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]].

quiz.q: Under 21.175, which aircraft receives a SPECIAL airworthiness certificate?
options: A primary category aircraft
A utility category airplane
An acrobatic category airplane
A normal category airplane
quiz.why: Primary, restricted, provisional and limited category aircraft get special certificates; normal, utility and acrobatic get standard ones [[60:66|14 CFR 21.175]].

quiz.q: An experimental certificate issued for research and development lasts how long, unless the FAA sets a shorter period?
options: 1 year
7 years
3 years
Unlimited
quiz.why: Experimental certificates for research and development, showing compliance, crew training or market survey are effective for 3 years from issue or renewal [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(4)]].

quiz.q: How long is a special flight permit effective?
options: 30 days
Until the next annual inspection
Until the aircraft lands at its destination, with no time limit
For the period of time specified in the permit
quiz.why: A special flight permit is effective for the period of time specified in the permit [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(2)]].

quiz.q: An annual inspection entry ends: "...a list of discrepancies and unairworthy items dated (date) has been provided for the aircraft owner." What does that tell you?
options: The aircraft was approved for return to service with minor items open
The aircraft was not approved for return to service at that inspection
Only the engine needs more work
The aircraft may fly for 10 more hours
quiz.why: That statement is used when the aircraft is not approved for return to service [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)(5)]].

quiz.q: Where can you get information about alternative methods of compliance the FAA has already approved for an AD?
options: Any A&P mechanic
The annual edition of 14 CFR Part 39
The aircraft manufacturer's latest service bulletin on the same subject
The office identified in the AD as responsible for approving AMOCs
quiz.why: Each AD names the office responsible for approving AMOCs, and that office can provide information on alternatives it has approved [[60:126|14 CFR 39.21]].

quiz.q: Under Part 43 Appendix A, which panel unit swap may a pilot owner do as preventive maintenance?
options: Swapping a tray-mounted nav or comm radio, with an operational check before use
Swapping a tray-mounted autopilot computer, as long as no wiring is touched at all
Swapping a tray-mounted transponder, followed by a ground test
Swapping a tray-mounted DME, since it is a standard part
quiz.why: Preventive maintenance includes removing and replacing tray-mounted panel navigation and communication units, but not automatic flight control systems, transponders or DME, and an operational check is required before the unit is used [[60:143|App. A(c)(31)]].

quiz.q: What does AC 91-67A say about the format of a KOEL?
options: It must follow the one standard format that the Part 23 certification rules set out
It is always a table in POH Section 2
There is no standard format, so manufacturers present it in various ways
It is the same document as the MMEL
quiz.why: The certification rules require the information, but there is no standard format [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]].

quiz.q: Operating under an MEL, which way of accessing the MEL and LOA is NOT acceptable to the PIC?
options: Having the chief pilot read it over the phone
A digital copy on an EFB in the airplane
A printed copy in the airplane
A printed copy in the seat-back pocket
quiz.why: The MEL may be printed or digital, but indirect access by telephone, radio or data link is not acceptable [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1]].

quiz.q: According to the AIH, when should an instructor determine the aircraft's official airworthiness status?
options: After engine start
Only at the start of each month, when the school's records are updated
Before scheduled flights and before conducting the actual preflight
Only when the learner asks
quiz.why: The instructor should determine official airworthiness status before scheduled flights and before conducting the preflight, and resolve questions with maintenance first [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: The last annual entry carries the discrepancy-list statement. Since then an A&P repaired the brake listed on it. The other listed item, a left position light, was placarded "Inoperative" by the inspector as allowed under 91.213(d)(2). What can your student fly?
options: Nothing until both items are fixed
Night only with a flashlight on board
Day or night, because the inspector placarded it as allowed under 91.213(d)(2)
Day VFR, if the other 91.213(d) conditions are met; not night
final_quiz.why: Inspectors placard items permitted to be inoperative under 91.213(d)(2) and list them [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]], so a day flight can be legal. Position lights are required at night [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's friend owns an airplane with a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category. Your learner asks whether it needs an annual inspection under 91.409. What do you teach?
options: Yes; every U.S. civil aircraft needs an annual within the preceding 12 calendar months
No; a light-sport aircraft needs only a 100-hour inspection, and only when used for hire
No; it needs no periodic inspection at all if the owner complies with all ADs
No; 91.327 requires a condition inspection every 12 calendar months instead
final_quiz.why: The annual and 100-hour rules of 91.409(a) and (b) do not apply to an aircraft with a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(c)(1)]]. Instead, 91.327 requires a condition inspection once every 12 calendar months by an appropriately rated repairman (light-sport), mechanic or repair station, and compliance with all applicable ADs [[60:518|14 CFR 91.327]].

final_quiz.q: A learner's amateur-built experimental airplane has an inoperative fuel flow display. The operating limitations say nothing about inoperative equipment. What is true?
options: Defer it under 91.213(d) like any non-turbine airplane
It may not be flown with the item inoperative, since that is not specifically authorized in its operating limitations
Experimental aircraft are exempt from all equipment rules
It may be flown day VFR only
final_quiz.why: An aircraft issued an original experimental certificate may not be operated with inoperative items unless specifically authorized in its operating limitations [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]].

final_quiz.q: On an MEL-equipped airplane, a light fails during taxi. The MEL allows the deferral with an (M) procedure requiring a mechanic's inspection. What now?
options: Take off now, and have the mechanic do the inspection at the destination airport
MEL relief has ended because the engine is running
No takeoff until the deferral, including the inspection, is complete
Treat it as an in-flight failure under the AFM
final_quiz.why: MEL relief applies up until takeoff, but an aircraft may not take off until the deferral process is complete, including a required inspection [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.1]] [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.2]].

final_quiz.q: A propeller was modified under an STC in exactly the area an AD covers, and the AD inspection can no longer be done as written. What must the owner do?
options: Nothing: the STC modification ends the AD's applicability to that propeller
Request FAA approval of an alternative method of compliance
Follow the propeller maker's service bulletin instead
Get a special flight permit for every flight
final_quiz.why: The AD still applies to a changed product [[60:125|14 CFR 39.15]], and if a change affects your ability to do the AD you must request an AMOC [[60:126|14 CFR 39.17]].

final_quiz.q: An owner needs to fly to a shop to do an AD. The AD states that special flight permits are not permitted. What is correct?
options: The FSDO must still issue a permit
No permit is available, so it may not fly there with the AD undone
The 10-hour allowance covers the trip
A permit may still be issued if a CFI signs the application as the pilot
final_quiz.why: The FSDO may issue a special flight permit for AD work unless the AD states otherwise [[60:126|14 CFR 39.23]], and operating with an unmet AD is a violation [[60:125|14 CFR 39.7]].

final_quiz.q: A recreational pilot owns her standard-category airplane and replaces its spark plugs. Under current 14 CFR, what is true?
options: She may do the work and also sign it off, since 43.3(g) covers every Part 61 pilot except sport pilots
She may neither do the work nor sign it off
She may do the work, but approving the return to service needs at least a private certificate
Only a sport pilot may do this on a standard-category airplane
final_quiz.why: Any Part 61 pilot certificate holder except a sport pilot may do preventive maintenance on an aircraft they own or operate [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]; 43.7(f) requires at least a private certificate to approve return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]].

final_quiz.q: Your flight school buys a used trainer whose standard airworthiness certificate was issued in 1998 for the first owner. Your student asks whether the school must apply for a new one. What is correct?
options: No; it transfers with the aircraft and has no printed expiration date
Yes; the school needs a new one before using the trainer for paid instruction
Yes; an airworthiness certificate ends when the aircraft is sold to a new owner
No, but the IA must reissue it with the new owner's data at the next annual
final_quiz.why: An airworthiness certificate is transferred with the aircraft [[60:66|14 CFR 21.179]]. A standard certificate has no printed expiry: it stays effective as long as the aircraft is registered in the United States and its maintenance, preventive maintenance and alterations follow Parts 43 and 91 [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]] [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Your student asks what an "Inoperative" placard must look like under the 91.213(d) guidance. Which answer is accurate?
options: Any form, if legible, visible to the crew, next to the control or indicator where practical, and not covering other controls
An FAA-printed red sticker
A note in the logbook is enough
Engraved, permanent marking
final_quiz.why: The placard need not be in a particular form, but it must be legible and visible, placed next to the control or indicator where practical, and must not obscure other controls [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]].

final_quiz.q: The sole registered owner of a club airplane, an individual, died six weeks ago. His family offers the airplane for a lesson. What about the registration?
options: Still effective until the estate sells the airplane or registers it anew
No longer effective: it ended 30 days after the holder's death
Effective for 90 days after death
Effective until it expires after seven years
final_quiz.why: A registration certificate is effective until, among other events, 30 days have elapsed since the death of the holder [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(a)(4)]]. An effective registration is required [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: The POH's KOEL lists the stall warning system as required for all kinds of operation. It fails on preflight; the airplane has no MEL and no shop on the field. Best plan?
options: Remove it as preventive maintenance
Defer it under 91.213(d) with a placard and a pilot's no-hazard finding, for day VFR only
Fly if the student promises to watch airspeed
It cannot be deferred; repair it, or fly it to a shop on a special flight permit
final_quiz.why: Equipment the KOEL requires may not be deferred for that operation [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(ii)]]; inoperative equipment may be flown under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

final_quiz.q: Three non-required items are legally deferred on the airplane for tonight's dual cross-country, and your student worked a full day first. What does AC 91-67A ask you to weigh before flying?
options: A safety risk analysis covering how the failures interact, night operations, workload and crew fatigue
Nothing more: legal deferrals mean the flight is safe
Only whether each item is placarded
Only the weather
final_quiz.why: The safety risk analysis includes the interrelationship of multiple failures, night operations, extra workload and crew fatigue [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]].

final_quiz.q: The club is selling an airplane. Which records does 91.417(b) say must be transferred with it?
options: Only the last annual inspection entry and the current registration certificate
Total time, life-limited parts, inspection and AD status, and major alteration forms
Every maintenance record ever made, since none may be discarded while the aircraft exists
None; the seller keeps them, and the buyer's mechanic opens a new set of logbooks
final_quiz.why: Records of maintenance, preventive maintenance and alteration work are kept until the work is repeated or superseded or for 1 year. The total time in service, current status of life-limited parts, time since overhaul, inspection status, AD status and major alteration forms are retained and transferred with the aircraft when it is sold [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)]] [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)]].

takeaways: Teach one sequence: papers, inspections and ADs, required equipment for this flight, then condition.
Determine the airplane's official status before the lesson, and do it with the learner, every time.
Read the inspection statement, not just the date; a signature approves only the work performed.
ADs are law with no overfly allowance; SAIBs are advice worth reading.
Preventive maintenance is only the Appendix A(c) list, and a pilot's sign-off on a standard airplane needs at least a private certificate.
Without an MEL, run all four 91.213(d)(2) tests, then remove or deactivate, placard, record and judge the hazard.
Legal is not safe: re-run the risk analysis whenever the flight changes, especially day to night.
cfi_notes: Preventive maintenance: PHAK 9-12 excludes student, sport and recreational pilots (sport pilots only on their own light-sport aircraft). Current 43.3(g) excludes only sport pilot certificate holders and names no other certificate level; student and recreational are Part 61 pilot certificates (61.5(a)(1)). 43.7(f) lets a person with at least a private certificate approve return to service after 43.3(g) work, and 43.7(h) lets at least a sport pilot approve an owned or operated light-sport aircraft; 43.7 gives student pilots no approval path. Teach the regulation text.

Deactivation: PHAK 9-10 says deactivation may be as simple as the pilot pulling a circuit breaker. AC 91-67A 4.2.2 says deactivation is not preventive maintenance, a switch does not remove power, and an authorized person must make the 43.9 entry. Teach the AC and the operator's own procedure.

Pink copy: PHAK 9-7 says the second copy of the registration application is good for 90 days. Current 47.31(c) has no 90-day limit (until the certificate arrives or the application is denied, and not for an application made 12 months or more after the first one following a transfer). Teach the regulation.

Classification: PHAK 9-8 lists special certificates as experimental, restricted, limited, provisional and LSA. Current 21.175 (amended 2025) also lists primary category and special flight permits as special, and adds special classes to standard. PHAK 3-2 includes primary. Teach 21.175.

Wording drift: AFH 2-3 says ELT inspection within the last 12 months and PHAK 9-9 says transponder within 24 months; 91.207(d) and 91.413(a) say calendar months. PHAK 9-8 describes the 100-hour as for carrying passengers for hire; 91.409(b) says any person other than a crewmember. Teach the CFR words.
PHAK 9-10 refers readers to AC 91-67, which was canceled on November 3, 2017 (AC 91-67A 1.4). Use AC 91-67A.

The only MEL page in these sources (AC 91-67A Figure 2-1) is a sample from a turbine airplane MMEL (flight data recorder items). Use it to teach the columns and symbols, then get the real MEL if your school has one.

Examiners change one fact at a time in S2 and S3: day to night, learner-provided to school-provided airplane, VFR to IFR. Drill your learners the same way and have them re-run the whole sequence each time.

If you instruct in airplanes you do not maintain, learn the operator's discrepancy-reporting system before your first lesson; the AIH names unawareness of inoperative equipment and overdue inspections as an instructor risk.
gaps: SAIBs appear in the sources only as two PHAK examples and the statement that they are not regulatory; how to search for them and how they are distributed is not covered (K1c).
No sample KOEL is in the sources. AC 91-67A 1.8.9 explains it but says there is no standard format; read the KOEL in your airplane's POH/AFM (K3c).
No small-airplane MEL sample is in the sources; the AC 91-67A example page comes from a turbine MMEL (K3b).
The special flight permit application form and its current submission method are not named in the sources; the PHAK says the local FSDO provides help and forms (K1d).
Which items on a particular airplane are required for certification, standard or optional comes only from that airplane's equipment list and POH/AFM.
How a school records discrepancies, who may deactivate items and what placards it uses are operator procedures; ask the school or owner.

activities.title: Match the certificate to its limit
activities.intro: Tap a certificate, then the operating limitation that goes with it.

pairs.r: The 91.205 instruments and equipment must be operable
Flown only for its special purpose, such as banner towing
Flown only for listed purposes such as crew training, market surveys or service testing
VFR day only unless the FAA authorizes otherwise
Effective only for the period stated on it

activities.title: True or false: ADs, SAIBs and the records
activities.intro: Your student makes these claims while you review the AD record together. True or false?

cards.s: Every AD is printed in full in the annual edition of 14 CFR.
cards.why: ADs are part of the CFR but not codified in the annual edition; they are published in the Federal Register as amendments to 39.13 [[60:125|14 CFR 39.13]].

cards.s: When an AD incorporates a manufacturer's service document, that document becomes part of the AD.
cards.why: A service document incorporated by reference becomes part of the AD [[60:126|14 CFR 39.27]].

cards.s: Flying three times with an unmet AD is three separate violations.
cards.why: You violate 39.7 each time you operate the aircraft [[60:125|14 CFR 39.9]].

cards.s: The AD record must show how each AD was complied with.
cards.why: The current AD status must include the method of compliance, AD number and revision date [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]].

cards.s: AD status and total time records may stay with the seller when the airplane is sold.
cards.why: The 91.417(a)(2) records, which include AD status and total time, are retained and transferred with the aircraft when it is sold [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(2)]].

cards.s: An emergency AD can require compliance before the next flight.
cards.why: ADs of an emergency nature require immediate compliance before further flight [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

activities.title: Get the out-of-annual airplane to the shop
activities.intro: A club airplane's annual has run out at a field with no inspector. Put the steps for a special flight permit in order.
steps: Confirm the flight fits a listed purpose: flying to a base where maintenance can be done
Contact the local FSDO for help and the forms
Submit the statement: purpose, itinerary, crew, how the airplane does not comply, and restrictions
Complete any inspection the FAA requires and record it in the aircraft records
Receive the permit and its operating limitations and carry them in the airplane
Fly only the permitted flight, within its limits and time period
activities.why: Purposes [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)(1)]]; FSDO help and the recorded inspection [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]; the statement and FAA inspections [[60:79|14 CFR 21.199]]; the permit lasts only its stated period [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(2)]].

activities.title: Who may do this work?
activities.intro: A private pilot owns the airplane. Sort each job.
buckets: Not preventive maintenance: needs authorized maintenance

items.t: Add air to a landing gear shock strut
Replace a cracked side window that does not touch structure or systems
Install different wheels when a weight and balance computation is needed
Deactivate an inoperative autopilot by securing its breaker
Update the panel GPS database from the flight deck, no tools, per the maker's instructions

activities.why: App. A(c)(3), (13), (17), (22) are on the list; (18) and (21) exclude the wheel and hydraulic jobs [[60:142|Part 43 App. A(c)]] [[60:143|App. A(c)(21)-(22)]]. Deactivation is not preventive maintenance [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. Qualifying database updates are not maintenance [[60:131|14 CFR 43.3(k)]].

activities.title: Read an MMEL page
activities.intro: Drag each name to its pin. Use the table key at the top right.

pins.label: Item not required by regulation, installed on some models
Proviso: conditions for flying with it inoperative

activities.why: System codes, the triple asterisk, the four columns and the remarks contents are explained in AC 91-67A [[58:15|AC 91-67A 2.2.1]] [[58:15|AC 91-67A 2.2.2]] [[58:16|AC 91-67A 2.2.4]] [[58:16|AC 91-67A 2.2.7]] [[58:16|AC 91-67A 2.2.9]]; (O) means an operations procedure [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.4.2]].

activities.title: Work out the numbers
activities.intro: Work it out from the rule, then type your answer.

items.q: The ELT transmitted for 41 minutes after an inadvertent activation and for 12 minutes during a search exercise. How many more minutes of use until its cumulative use reaches 1 hour, after which the battery must be replaced?
items.why: Batteries must be replaced when the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)(1)]]. 60 - (41 + 12) = 60 - 53 = 7 minutes.

items.q: The ELT was removed for repair on August 20, 2026, with the entry and the "ELT not installed" placard. Counting 90 days from removal, on what day of November 2026 does the 90-day limit end?
items.why: No person may operate the aircraft more than 90 days after the ELT is initially removed [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(10)]]. August 20 + 90 days: 11 days left in August, 30 in September, 31 in October = 72, plus 18 = 90, so November 18.

items.q: The school's airplane, used for paid instruction it provides, received an annual inspection at 3,018.2 hours time in service. At what time in service is the next 100-hour inspection due?
items.why: The airplane must have had an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. 3,018.2 + 100 = 3,118.2.

items.q: The school ends its progressive inspection program. The last complete inspection under it was finished at 4,206.3 hours. At what time in service is the 100-hour due?
items.why: After discontinuance, the 100-hour is due within 100 hours after that complete inspection [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(d)]]. 4,206.3 + 100 = 4,306.3.

items.q: An operator's MEL uses the generic Single-Engine Airplanes MMEL. A model-specific MMEL is published on March 5, 2026. The MEL must be revised within 90 calendar days. On what day of June 2026 is that?
items.why: The MEL must conform to the new model-specific MMEL within 90 calendar days of its publication [[58:14|AC 91-67A 2.1.2]]. March 5 + 90 days: 26 days left in March, 30 in April, 31 in May = 87, plus 3 = 90, so June 3.

items.q: A registered airplane with a paper certificate was destroyed in a hangar fire on September 18, 2026. Within 21 days the certificate must go back to the Registry. What is the last day of October 2026 for that?
items.why: Registration ends when the aircraft is totally destroyed [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(a)(2)]], and the holder returns the certificate within 21 days [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(b)(3)]]. September 18 + 21 days: 12 days left in September, plus 9 = 21, so October 9.

activities.title: Night cross-country at the flight school
activities.intro: You will give paid dual tonight in the school's Cessna 172 (non-turbine, no MEL), on a night cross-country to an airport 85 NM away. You start the airworthiness review with your student at 4 p.m.

steps.s: The status board shows the ELT was removed for repair 40 days ago. The logbook has the removal entry and an "ELT not installed" placard is in view. What do you teach?
options: No-go: an ELT is required on any flight that goes beyond 50 NM from the departure airport
Legal: the ELT is temporarily removed with the entry and placard, within 90 days
No-go: a removed ELT may stay out only 30 days, so at 40 days the airplane cannot be flown
No-go unless only the required crew are aboard, even though the entry and placard are there
steps.why: During a temporary removal, the ELT requirement does not apply if the records entry and placard are there and no more than 90 days have passed [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(10)]].

steps.s: The discrepancy sheet shows "left position light inop", written up this morning. Nothing is placarded. What now?
options: Defer it under 91.213(d) and go, since the right light still works
Only the right light is required, so the flight can go with the left one inoperative
Carry a flashlight instead and show it to any aircraft that approaches from the left
It is required at night, so repair it before tonight's flight, or change the lesson to day
steps.why: Position lights are required for night VFR [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(2)]], so the item fails the (d)(2) test for this operation [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

steps.s: A mechanic replaces the bulb and signs it off. On the runup the autopilot fails its self-test. It is not required for this flight by any rule, list or AD. Your student reaches for its breaker.
options: Taxi back: an authorized person deactivates, placards and logs it (43.9), then the hazard and risk check
Pull it and go: securing a breaker is preventive maintenance, so the student may do it and the flight can proceed
Ignore it and just do not engage it, since the autopilot is not required for this flight by any rule or list
Cancel the flight: autopilots can never be deferred, so any failed self-test grounds the airplane until it is repaired
steps.why: Under 91.213(d)(3) it must be deactivated and placarded; deactivation is not preventive maintenance and needs an authorized person's 43.9 entry [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]] [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. Then the (d)(4) hazard determination [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]].

steps.s: It is now 8:30 p.m. Two items were worked on today, you are both tired, and the destination is forecast marginal VFR. Your student still wants to go.
options: Go: everything is now legal, both items worked on today were signed off, and the destination is still forecast VFR
Go, but let the student fly the whole flight while you rest your eyes in the right seat to recover from fatigue
Coach the risk analysis: night, fatigue and a marginal destination point to pattern work or a reschedule
Go and decide en route whether to divert, using the fuel on board and the weather updates as the flight goes on
steps.why: The AC 91-67A risk analysis covers night operations, workload, crew fatigue and the destination environment [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]. The AIH suggests changing the plan to stay in the pattern, using a simulator or ground lesson, or rescheduling [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
